RELEVANT CHARACTER BACKGROUND

Amina Adebayo lives in a rented room in Mushin, a dense Lagos neighborhood. She works as a day laborer sweeping rubble at a building site for 500 naira per day, with no guarantee that work will be available tomorrow. In the afternoon, she attends a vocational carpentry course, where she is the only woman in the class. She sits near the back, watches the instructor’s hands more than his words, and waits for the right moment to ask questions she has already mentally rehearsed. She keeps a worn notebook in which she records every expense with precision, including 50 naira for a sachet of water, 100 for groundnuts, and 200 for a fresh notebook leaf. Her tools—a hammer, a chisel, and a small saw—are stored in a locked metal box under her bed. She oils the box hinges every Friday evening, a ritual her late father taught her before he died of a fever when she was twelve.

Since her father’s death, Amina has relied on the order she imposes on herself: double-checking measurements before cutting, triple-checking the lock on the tool box, and counting each day’s coins until they can be translated into rent, food, or an extra lesson. She values thrift as necessity rather than virtue, but she privately wishes to be generous and sometimes gives extra food to a neighbor’s child. Even so, every kobo she gives away feels like a loss against an uncertain future. Her faith is quiet; she prays in the morning not for riches but for protection from accidents, broken tools, and illness. She speaks Yoruba with her landlady and Pidgin at the site, but writes in careful, school-learned English because she once heard it could open a door. She does not laugh easily, though she smiles privately when Emeka, a quiet older trainee, taps his foot in rhythm without noticing.

Her mother lives in Ibadan and sends notes only for urgent family events; she expects Amina to maintain family ties despite distance. Her aunt, her mother’s elder sister, values large family gatherings and will notice Amina’s absence. Emeka sometimes shares his offcuts with Amina and has become a silent ally in the workshop. When faced with competing obligations in the past, Amina once skipped a family wedding to attend an extra carpentry session and later sent a small gift. She regularly postpones minor purchases, such as replacing a worn sandal, to keep her tool fund intact. She must cover rent, food, lessons, and tool upkeep from limited and unpredictable day-labor earnings. She remains committed to the weekly Friday ritual of oiling her tools, learned from her late father.

OBJECTIVE SITUATION

After her morning sweep, Amina’s landlady stops her in the courtyard and hands her a folded note from Amina’s mother. The note announces that her cousin’s baby will be named next Saturday in Ibadan, and her aunt expects her to attend. The ceremony will last all day. Attending would require Amina to miss her carpentry class and pay for transport. She has only a few days to reply. Her mother writes that Amina can borrow a lace blouse from her sister. Amina’s tools need oil that weekend, and she cannot afford both the trip and a new chisel. She stands by the gate with the note in her hand.

PRE-APPRAISAL STATE AND ACCESSIBLE MEMORIES

Amina has just finished sweeping rubble and is breathing heavily. The morning heat already beads sweat on her forehead. Her hands are calloused and slightly sore from gripping the broom handle, and she is hungry, having eaten only a piece of leftover garri before dawn. The note’s handwriting—her mother’s rounded letters—reminds her of the day her father died, when her mother wrote the same careful script to tell the school she would not return. The phrase “naming ceremony” recalls her own first day at the carpentry class, when she introduced herself and no one replied.
